questions.q: In the Schrödinger equation iħ d|ψ⟩/dt = H|ψ⟩, what role does the Hamiltonian H play?
options: It is the operator that generates time evolution -- it fully determines how the state changes over time, and its eigenvalues are the system's possible energies
It is a measurement operator that collapses the state whenever applied
It is a normalization constant with no physical meaning
It represents the classical probability of the system's current state
questions.explain: H is the Hermitian operator encoding everything about how a system evolves in time; knowing H and the current state tells you the system's entire future evolution, and H's eigenvalues/eigenvectors give the system's energies and definite-energy states.

questions.q: Why does the linearity of the Schrödinger equation matter for superposition?
options: It guarantees that if |ψ1⟩ and |ψ2⟩ are valid solutions, any superposition of them is also a valid solution -- meaning ordinary time evolution preserves superposition rather than collapsing it
It means the equation can only be solved for classical, non-superposed states
It guarantees that every state eventually evolves into a single definite basis state
Linearity has no particular significance for superposition
questions.explain: Linearity is exactly what lets a superposition remain a superposition (generally a different one) as it evolves under the Schrödinger equation -- ordinary evolution never collapses a state on its own; only measurement does.

questions.q: How is the linearity used in this lesson connected to the no-cloning theorem proof from Chapter 5?
options: The no-cloning proof relied on exactly the same linearity property -- that a unitary (and therefore Schrödinger-equation-consistent) operator applied to a superposition acts as the same combination of its action on each basis term
The two topics are entirely unrelated mathematical ideas that happen to share vocabulary
No-cloning actually disproves the linearity of the Schrödinger equation
Linearity only applies to single-qubit states, while no-cloning only concerns multi-qubit states
questions.explain: The no-cloning proof depended on a hypothetical cloning unitary acting linearly on a superposition, producing a contradiction. That's the identical linearity property central to this lesson -- the same underlying structural fact about quantum operators showing up in two different arguments.

questions.q: Why is ordinary time evolution under the Schrödinger equation described as a 'genuinely different process' from measurement?
options: Time evolution is deterministic and linear, preserving superposition, while measurement is probabilistic and collapses the state to a single outcome -- they are not the same kind of process at all
They are actually the same process, just described with different vocabulary
Time evolution only applies to classical systems, while measurement only applies to quantum systems
Measurement is a special case of time evolution under a particular Hamiltonian
questions.explain: Ordinary evolution under H is deterministic and linear (superposition-preserving), while measurement (Chapter 3) is probabilistic and collapses the state -- two structurally different processes governing a quantum system.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are quantum gates, physically, in terms of the Schrödinger equation?
options: A snapshot of Schrödinger-equation evolution under a deliberately engineered Hamiltonian, applied for a precise duration
An abstraction layered entirely on top of physics, with no connection to the Schrödinger equation
A classical logic operation that happens to be renamed for quantum computers
A measurement operation disguised as a unitary matrix
questions.explain: Gates aren't abstractions bolted onto physics -- physically, applying a gate means letting a qubit evolve under an engineered Hamiltonian for a specific time, so that the resulting U(t) matches the desired gate matrix, as Lesson 26 and Lesson 28 make concrete.
